summary:
CropCompass helps farmers and agricultural advisers answer a practical question: what should I plant next? Built for Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data, it combines NASA POWER weather history, MODIS vegetation observations, SoilGrids estimates, and farmer-entered crop records to compare next-season crops and two-year rotations.

Users choose priorities for income, water savings, soil health, and risk, then explore simulated yield ranges, indicative economics, irrigation needs, and historical failure counts. Interactive field previews make soil and water assumptions visible; crop journals and saved plans retain decision context. English, Hindi, Telugu, guided tours, guest access, and the optional Sprout assistant make the evidence easier to explore.

The goal is more transparent, better-informed planning, especially where water is constrained. CropCompass currently uses an India-specific crop pack. It is a decision-support prototype, not a forecast or guaranteed prescription: modelled outcomes and costs require local validation, and source-readiness and confidence labels disclose incomplete data and assumptions.
details:
CROPCOMPASS: EARTH DATA FOR THE NEXT CROP DECISION

THE PROBLEM
Farmers balance rainfall timing, irrigation access, income, soil condition and the effects of previous crops. A high-ranked crop is not necessarily suitable for a particular field or water supply. CropCompass brings scattered environmental data into one workflow so farmers and advisers can compare those trade-offs rather than receive an unexplained prescription.

WHAT WE BUILT
CropCompass is a working web-based crop-planning prototype. Users locate a farm by coordinates, map pin or drawn boundary; record crops, dates and management history; review climate, soil and vegetation data; and explore the next crop or a two-year rotation. They can override known soil values, select rain-fed, protective or full irrigation, and weight income, water savings, soil health and risk. Results include modelled yield distributions, indicative profit, irrigation demand, sowing windows and historical failure counts. Field previews show the crop and root zone while labelling assumed depth and modelled soil water. Saved plans retain the chosen scenario and provenance.

HOW NASA DATA IS USED
NASA POWER daily weather history, beginning in 1981 where variables are available, supports climate summaries, evapotranspiration and historical crop-water trials. Annual downloads are checked for coverage, units and physical plausibility, with same-provider monthly consistency checks and resumable checkpoints. NASA MODIS Terra MOD13Q1 NDVI, obtained through the ORNL DAAC REST subset service, supplies 250 m, 16-day vegetation histories and approximate growing-season dates for farmer confirmation. NDVI does not identify crops automatically. SoilGrids predictions and the farmer's journal add soil and crop-rotation context. A drawn boundary does not make coarse weather data field-resolution.

MODELS AND DECISION LOGIC
A deterministic Python engine uses FAO-56-style evapotranspiration and daily soil-water accounting, FAO-33-style yield response, Saxton-Rawls-style soil-water relationships, and RothC-style carbon estimates. It applies crop calendars, crop-family and shared-host succession rules, and flowering/heat adjustments. It replays historical weather to compare distributions, not to forecast a guaranteed season. Failure means simulated yield below half attainable yield, not observed farm bankruptcy. Soil-water state is modelled, not measured groundwater. The default 1 m profile is an explicit assumption unless the farmer supplies a known value.

CREATIVITY AND ACCESS
The distinctive contribution is connecting Earth data with previous crops, water availability and user priorities, then making the assumptions visible in the same decision workflow. The crop-journey dashboard, interactive field cross-section, separate source-readiness indicators, saved-plan warnings and scenario comparisons make technical evidence easier to question and interpret. English, Hindi and Telugu interfaces, guided tours and convertible guest sessions reduce barriers to exploration. Sprout explains selected application evidence through an optional, consent-based conversational interface.

TOOLS AND ARCHITECTURE
The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, React Router, TanStack Query, i18next, Leaflet, Apache ECharts and Lucide. The backend uses Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLAlchemy, Alembic, psycopg, NumPy, pandas, PyYAML and zstandard. Vercel hosts the frontend, Render hosts the API, and Neon PostgreSQL stores application data. Mailjet/SMTP supports password-reset email when configured. Password hashing, ownership checks and account export/deletion controls protect private farm records. No dedicated field hardware is required. Source: https://github.com/Praannjaal/CropCompass

SI/AI DISCLOSURE
GitHub Copilot and Claude assisted research, coding, debugging, interpretation of test/model outputs, translation, interface design and documentation. The team remains responsible for reviewing the results. Sprout uses a Groq-hosted language model through an OpenAI-compatible SDK; the source default is openai/gpt-oss-120b. It explains bounded evidence, while the deterministic engine computes numerical crop results. CropCompass is not a trained machine-learning crop predictor. The Sprout artwork is generated by project code; UI design and presentation preparation were AI-assisted. AI output can be incorrect and needs human review.

INTENDED IMPACT AND LIMITATIONS
The intended beneficiaries are farmers and agricultural advisers, initially within the India crop pack. The intended benefit is better-informed discussion and transparent comparison, not a measured claim of higher yields, profits, water savings or carbon sequestration. Prices and costs are indicative rather than live market feeds. Historical frequencies and sensitivity tests are not calibrated future probabilities. Satellite downloads may be partial or unavailable and are labelled independently from weather and planning readiness. Standard soil defaults are identified when mapped inputs are missing. When recent weather cannot be verified, eligible planning can use an explicitly low-confidence historical-reference scenario; substituted recent days are excluded from historical trials. Next steps are calibration against local field observations, agronomist review, farmer usability evaluation, native-language review and responsible expansion of regional crop packs. No NASA endorsement is implied.

ADDITIONAL SOFTWARE AND RESOURCE ATTRIBUTION
Software is grouped through the public frontend/backend manifests and detailed attribution inventory to fit the form's resource-row limit. Supporting packages include React DOM, react-i18next, pydantic-settings, email-validator, argon2-cffi, PyYAML, python-zstandard, eventsource-parser, the OpenAI Python SDK, DefinitelyTyped, pytest and Ruff. Their provider and license references are recorded in the linked inventory. The OpenAI SDK is used as a Groq-compatible client, not as evidence of using OpenAI's hosted API.

Design references discovered with Inspo MCP: https://coda.io/ ; https://ghost.org/ ; https://trello.com/ . The project's own screenshots, drawing code and SI disclosure identify presentation and artwork provenance.
